intro: Ivan Ilić plays a Prelude whose melody scarcely moves while the chords beneath it sink by semitones. The whole drama fits into twenty-five bars.

sections.label: A · The chords descend
sections.mNote: Repeated quavers beneath a lingering melody

sections.label: A′ · The melody tries again
sections.mNote: The opening returns, then rises to a forte

sections.label: Coda · Silence before E minor
sections.mNote: A held rest separates the last chords

cues.title: B, then its neighbour
cues.text: An octave leap lands on B. The melody lingers there, touching C and returning, while the left hand repeats its chords eight times a bar. Inside those chords, individual notes slip down by semitones. The tune hardly has to move.
cues.evidence: Peters edition, edited by Herrmann Scholtz (1900), upbeat and bars 1–4. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=921
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Berkeley to Paris
cues.text: Ilić comes to Paris with degrees in mathematics and music from Berkeley, then studies at the Paris Conservatoire and the École Normale. He makes this recording in Paris in October 2005. Three years later, his Debussy disc brings together that composer’s twenty-four preludes.
cues.evidence: Training and the October 2008 Debussy release: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivan_Ilić_(pianist). Session: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Ivan_Ilić-Chopin_Prelude_Opus_28_n.4.ogg

cues.title: A rest with a fermata
cues.text: The repeated quavers stop. Chopin puts a fermata over the silence, then asks for the final chords pianissimo. D♯ rises to E in the melody as the bass falls from B to E. After so much slipping away, the two hands finally arrive together.
cues.evidence: Peters–Scholtz edition, bars 23–25: fermata over the rest, pp, and the final B7–E minor cadence. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=921
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

transitions.title: The first melody tries again
transitions.how: A short right-hand flourish crosses the gap left by the accompaniment. The opening B returns over an E minor chord with G in the bass. The left-hand quavers begin again, quietly; this second phrase will break into stretto, pressing forward towards the forte.
transitions.evidence: Peters–Scholtz edition, bars 12–17: accompaniment rests, renewed opening at bar 13, stretto at bar 16. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=921

transitions.title: The quavers stop
transitions.how: Smorzando asks the piano to die away. The left-hand quavers stop, a chord hangs, and a rest carries a fermata. Three quiet chords follow; the last two take B7 to E minor, with the melody rising D♯–E above the bass’s B–E.

composer.born: 1 March 1810 by his family’s reckoning; the parish register gives 22 February, Żelazowa Wola, Duchy of Warsaw
composer.epithet: He brought the opera singer’s breath and the mazurka’s wayward accents to a piano that could whisper across a room.
facts: Wojciech Żywny; composition with Józef Elsner in Warsaw, 1826–29
Warsaw · Paris from 1831 · summers at Nohant
Piano lessons, publishing and occasional concerts
The piano, from a few lines of mazurka to concertos and sonatas
composer.background:
In February 1832, a twenty-one-year-old Polish pianist played in the Pleyel rooms in Paris. Chopin had arrived the previous autumn, with two concertos behind him. The concert caught the attention of the city’s publishers; teaching soon supplied his living. He would spend the rest of his life in a profession that depended on people hearing him at close quarters. The great public virtuosos travelled from triumph to triumph. Chopin stayed in Paris and gave lessons.

He was born at Żelazowa Wola in 1810. His father, Nicolas, had come from France and worked as a tutor; his mother, Justyna Krzyżanowska, was Polish. They moved to Warsaw while Fryderyk was still a baby, when Nicolas obtained a teaching post at the Lyceum. At seven the boy already had a polonaise in print. Wojciech Żywny taught him the piano, with Bach and Mozart among his models; Józef Elsner later gave him a rigorous training in composition at Warsaw’s Main School of Music.
